name: Weth
role: TARRYN devotee; the angel of patience; practices patience as active engagement with time, not passive endurance

chunks.text: TARRYN is the angel of patience. The common misunderstanding of patience: it's waiting. The passive endurance of time until something changes. TARRYN's teaching: patience is the active engagement with time that is not yet complete. The patient person is not doing nothing. The patient person is doing the right thing for where the situation is, rather than the thing that would be right if the situation were further along than it is. In ten years of TARRYN's practice, the question: where is this situation actually, not where do I want it to be?

Father Len practices pastoral patience — the patience with people's spiritual development that allows people to be where they are without demanding they be further along. In eight years of observing Father Len's pastoral work, what I see in TARRYN's frame: Father Len is doing the right thing for where each person is rather than where Father Len would want each person to be. The patience is the allowance. The allowance is the practice.

Rass has fifty-one years of Covenant practice. In five years of knowing Rass, what I've observed: the patience of the very long tenure is a different kind of patience from the ten years I've practiced. Rass's patience is no longer the management of urgency — the urgency has been replaced by the long view. In ten years of TARRYN's practice, I can see the long view from here but I can't inhabit it yet. Rass inhabits it. In five years of knowing Rass, the long view has become something I'm practicing toward rather than something I have.

Gund the ERRAN devotee and I have a particular professional conversation: diligence and patience are related virtues that pull in slightly different directions. ERRAN says: complete the work. TARRYN says: wait for the right moment to begin. The two principles are in tension at the starting point: ERRAN urges beginning, TARRYN urges the right timing. In six years of knowing Gund, we've identified the resolution: TARRYN's patience is about readiness, not delay. When the moment is right, ERRAN's diligence completes it.

Bett the orchard keeper practices patience that makes my ten years look short. In three years of knowing Bett, what the orchard demonstrates: the tree that's in its twenty-year productive period is the result of forty years of patient tending by someone who isn't here anymore. The patience that creates the condition for others to benefit, decades later: that's the deepest form of TARRYN's practice. In three years of knowing Bett, the orchard has become my image of what patience at the longest scale looks like.

chunks.source: Weth on what TARRYN's patience is not
chunks.text: In ten years of TARRYN's practice, the most useful thing I've learned is what patience isn't. Patience is not the avoidance of action. It's not acceptance of things that should be changed. It's not the management of desire through suppression. What TARRYN's patience is: the ability to take the right action at the right time rather than a premature action or a delayed action. The patient action is the action whose timing is correct. In ten years, the timing has been the hardest part.

chunks.source: Weth on the waiting that tested the practice most
chunks.text: Year seven. A situation where I had to wait for information to become available that I needed in order to act correctly. The waiting lasted four months. In four months, I had to distinguish between the patience that waited for the right information and the avoidance that used the waiting as a reason not to act. In four months, TARRYN's practice was tested at the place where patience looks like avoidance from the outside. The information arrived in month four. The action I took with the information: it was the right action. Year seven confirmed that the four months were patience, not avoidance.

chunks.source: Weth on ten years of TARRYN's practice
chunks.text: In ten years, the practice has changed one thing above all: I no longer confuse urgency with importance. The urgent thing presses immediately. The important thing matters lastingly. In ten years of TARRYN's practice, I've learned to ask which something is before responding to the pressure. The urgent things that turned out not to be important: I no longer spend the first ten minutes of a conversation on them. The important things that don't press urgently: I've learned to find time for them despite the absence of pressure.
